items.original_text: Filing step: Register the business with the SF Treasurer & Tax Collector to obtain a Business Account Number (BAN), and file a Fictitious Business Name statement with the SF County Clerk if the public-facing name differs from the entity name. What to say: Submit the Business Registration application online at sftreasurer.org with the EIN and entity documents; the BAN is issued in 1–5 days ($55–$700 tiered by gross receipts, plus $4 state fee). File the FBN statement in person or by mail with photo ID, then publish once a week for four weeks in a court-approved newspaper and file proof of publication within 45 days. Every other city department asks for the BAN.

What to say: Email the Entertainment Commission Deputy Director at entertainment.commission@sfgov.org to confirm eligibility: for live music, DJs or amplified sound until 1 a.m., a Place of Entertainment permit is likely required. items.original_text: Filing step: Once the CUA is approved by the Planning Commission (and any appeal period has passed), file the ABC Type 42 premises-to-premises transfer application with the California Department of Alcoholic Beverage Control. What to say: Submit the ABC transfer application (ABC-257) online at abc.ca.gov with the source bar's license number, the signed purchase agreement, a copy of the approved CUA motion, the seller's permit, proof of the entity and FBN, a signed lease at 995 Valencia, and the $1,000–$1,600 application fee. ABC will route the application to SF Planning and SFPD for zoning and public-safety review, post a 30-day public notice at the premises, and conduct an investigation. If the census tract is over-concentrated, Planning will prepare a Public Convenience or Necessity recommendation for the Board of Supervisors; coordinate with Planning's ABC liaison to expedite that referral. Budget 60–150 days for the transfer if unprotested, longer if a PCN hearing is required.

items.original_text: Filing step: File the Department of Public Health plan check application for the limited kitchen, and in parallel file the building permit application with DBI for tenant improvements and change of use, attaching the approved CUA motion. What to say: Submit the DPH plan check application online at sfdph.org/ehservices with the BAN, the Location ID (LIN), scaled drawings of the kitchen layout, equipment list, menu, and finishes; pay the $828–$2,207 plan-check fee. DPH will route the application to Planning (already approved via CUA) and assign a plan reviewer; schedule a pre-application meeting with the reviewer. In parallel, submit the building permit application at sf.gov/permitSF with the approved CUA motion, architectural plans stamped by a licensed architect, the DPH plan-check approval, and the fee (percentage of construction valuation, typically $800–$15,000). DBI will route the permit to Planning, Fire, Public Health and PUC for review (2–4 months for full plan review). Licensed subcontractors pull separate electrical, plumbing and mechanical permits.

items.original_text: Filing step: Schedule and pass the DPH pre-opening inspection, then apply for the Health Permit to Operate; in parallel, schedule the Fire Department Place of Assembly inspection (if occupancy is 50+) and the final DBI inspection. What to say: When construction is ~80% complete, contact your DPH plan reviewer to schedule a pre-final inspection at least two weeks in advance; address any deficiencies (missing hand sinks, unsealed surfaces, no hot water are common failures). Once the space passes, apply for the Permit to Operate online with the BAN, LIN, federal tax ID and the food safety manager certificate; pay the $470 application fee (no annual license fee for restaurants in FY 2026–28). DPH issues the permit after the final inspection. If occupancy is 50+, schedule a Fire Department Place of Assembly inspection and obtain the occupancy placard ($446 permit fee). Schedule the final DBI inspection; the building permit is finalized when all departments sign off.

items.original_text: Filing step: Before opening, register all alcohol servers and managers for California RBS (Responsible Beverage Service) training, subscribe to ASCAP and BMI music licenses, and set up workers' compensation insurance and EDD employer registration. What to say: All alcohol servers and managers must complete RBS certification within 60 days of hire: register on the ABC RBS Portal ($3), complete an approved course ($10–$25), pass the exam, and keep the certification list on site. Subscribe to ASCAP and BMI blanket licenses for live and recorded music (formula-based fees, typically $300–$2,500/year each, sign up at ascap.com and bmi.com). Obtain workers' compensation insurance from a licensed carrier or State Fund (premiums are 2–6% of payroll for restaurant class codes, no government fee); the health and entertainment permits ask for proof of coverage. Register as an employer with EDD at edd.ca.gov within 15 days of paying wages (free, online, 1–7 days).

items.original_text: Estimated time: 120 to 300 days. Estimated government cost: $6,278 to $21,100. Notes: The day range (120–300 days) and cost range ($6,278–$21,100 in government and application fees) cover the time and fees to obtain the four approvals in the entitlement path when they are granted: Conditional Use Authorization (120–300 days, $3,100–$15,000 per the catalog), Place of Entertainment or Limited Live Performance permit (45–120 days, $2,708–$3,800), Health Permit to Operate (14–45 days, $470–$1,000), and Building Permit with change of use (14–120 days, $800–$15,000). The CUA timeline is the critical path and runs in parallel with the Entertainment Commission permit; the ABC Type 42 license transfer (60–150 days, $1,000–$1,600) begins after CUA approval and runs in parallel with building construction, so it is not added to the day range but its fee is included in a separate alcohol-license line item. The ranges assume the CUA is approved and no appeal is filed; a denial, withdrawal or appeal adds months and is not a time to approval. The cost range includes only government fees and permit application fees; it does not include the cost to purchase the Type 42 license from the source bar (market price, typically $5,000–$50,000+ depending on seller and negotiation), architect and engineering fees for plans ($10,000–$30,000+), construction costs ($50,000–$150,000+ for kitchen, bar, finishes and ADA upgrades), license broker fees (10–15% of license purchase price if used), or legal counsel. ABC's undue-concentration test for census tract 208.01 (28 licenses against 12 authorized) may trigger a Public Convenience or Necessity hearing before the Board of Supervisors, adding 2–4 months; confirm the PCN requirement with SF Planning's ABC liaison before filing.

items.original_text: Filing step: Once the CUA is approved by the Planning Commission (and any appeal period has passed), file the ABC Type 42 premises-to-premises transfer application with the California Department of Alcoholic Beverage Control. What to say: Submit the ABC transfer application (ABC-257) online at abc.ca.gov with the source bar's license number, the signed purchase agreement, a copy of the approved CUA motion, the seller's permit, proof of the entity and FBN, a signed lease at 995 Valencia, and the $1,000–$1,600 application fee. ABC will route the application to SF Planning and SFPD for zoning and public-safety review, post a 30-day public notice at the premises, and conduct an investigation. If the census tract is over-concentrated, Planning will prepare a Public Convenience or Necessity recommendation for the Board of Supervisors; coordinate with Planning's ABC liaison to expedite that referral. Budget 60–150 days for the transfer if unprotested, longer if a PCN hearing is required.

items.original_text: Estimated time: 120 to 300 days. Estimated government cost: $6,278 to $21,100. Notes: The day range (120–300 days) and cost range ($6,278–$21,100 in government and application fees) cover the time and fees to obtain the four approvals in the entitlement path when they are granted: Conditional Use Authorization (120–300 days, $3,100–$15,000 per the catalog), Place of Entertainment or Limited Live Performance permit (45–120 days, $2,708–$3,800), Health Permit to Operate (14–45 days, $470–$1,000), and Building Permit with change of use (14–120 days, $800–$15,000). The CUA timeline is the critical path and runs in parallel with the Entertainment Commission permit; the ABC Type 42 license transfer (60–150 days, $1,000–$1,600) begins after CUA approval and runs in parallel with building construction, so it is not added to the day range but its fee is included in a separate alcohol-license line item. The ranges assume the CUA is approved and no appeal is filed; a denial, withdrawal or appeal adds months and is not a time to approval. The cost range includes only government fees and permit application fees; it does not include the cost to purchase the Type 42 license from the source bar (market price, typically $5,000–$50,000+ depending on seller and negotiation), architect and engineering fees for plans ($10,000–$30,000+), construction costs ($50,000–$150,000+ for kitchen, bar, finishes and ADA upgrades), license broker fees (10–15% of license purchase price if used), or legal counsel. ABC's undue-concentration test for census tract 208.01 (28 licenses against 12 authorized) may trigger a Public Convenience or Necessity hearing before the Board of Supervisors, adding 2–4 months; confirm the PCN requirement with SF Planning's ABC liaison before filing.

What to say: Submit the Business Registration application online at sftreasurer.org with the EIN and entity documents; the BAN is issued in 1–5 days ($55–$700 tiered by gross receipts, plus $4 state fee). File the FBN statement in person or by mail with photo ID, then publish once a week for four weeks in a court-approved newspaper and file proof of publication within 45 days. Every other city department asks for the BAN.

outcomes.original: Filing step: File the Conditional Use Authorization application with SF Planning, disclosing the bar use, the Type 42 license source (source bar's address and license number within the Mission SUD), the entertainment program, the floor area, and whether the business is formula retail. What to say: Submit the CUA application online at sf.gov/departments/planning with the BAN, project description (40-seat wine bar, limited kitchen, live entertainment and amplified sound until 1 a.m., Type 42 license transferred from [source bar name and address] within the Mission SUD), floor plans showing the bar area, seating, kitchen and performance area, and a Good Neighbor policy draft addressing § 202.2 and § 249.60(d) requirements (exterior lighting, 33% window signage, 50% clear glazing). Pay the CUA application fee ($3,100–$15,000 depending on construction cost; ask about First Year Free waivers for new storefront businesses). Planning will schedule a pre-application meeting, environmental review, a 300-foot mailed notice, a posted notice for 30 days, and a Commission hearing.
outcomes.note: Records mention posted notice and good-neighbor conditions but not the 30-day posting period, § 249.60(d) subsection, or specific lighting/signage percentages.

outcomes.original: Filing step: In parallel with the CUA application, determine whether the entertainment requires a Place of Entertainment permit or a Limited Live Performance permit, and file the appropriate Entertainment Commission application. What to say: Email the Entertainment Commission Deputy Director at entertainment.commission@sfgov.org to confirm eligibility: for live music, DJs or amplified sound until 1 a.m., a Place of Entertainment permit is likely required. File the POE application online with the BAN, a lease or proof of control, the floor plan showing the performance area and occupancy, and the Good Neighbor policy. Pay the $2,708 application fee (FY 2026–27). The application is routed to Police, Planning, Public Health and Fire for review, and a 30-day posted notice is required before the Commission hearing. The POE application should be filed after or at the same time as the CUA so that Planning's CUA approval is in hand when the Commission hears the POE.
outcomes.note: Record states $2,708 fee and 30-day posted notice but doesn't give the email, filing method, specific documents, all review agencies (only Police and Planning mentioned), or CUA timing advice.

outcomes.original: Filing step: Once the CUA is approved by the Planning Commission (and any appeal period has passed), file the ABC Type 42 premises-to-premises transfer application with the California Department of Alcoholic Beverage Control. What to say: Submit the ABC transfer application (ABC-257) online at abc.ca.gov with the source bar's license number, the signed purchase agreement, a copy of the approved CUA motion, the seller's permit, proof of the entity and FBN, a signed lease at 995 Valencia, and the $1,000–$1,600 application fee. ABC will route the application to SF Planning and SFPD for zoning and public-safety review, post a 30-day public notice at the premises, and conduct an investigation. If the census tract is over-concentrated, Planning will prepare a Public Convenience or Necessity recommendation for the Board of Supervisors; coordinate with Planning's ABC liaison to expedite that referral. Budget 60–150 days for the transfer if unprotested, longer if a PCN hearing is required.

outcomes.original: Filing step: File the Department of Public Health plan check application for the limited kitchen, and in parallel file the building permit application with DBI for tenant improvements and change of use, attaching the approved CUA motion. What to say: Submit the DPH plan check application online at sfdph.org/ehservices with the BAN, the Location ID (LIN), scaled drawings of the kitchen layout, equipment list, menu, and finishes; pay the $828–$2,207 plan-check fee. DPH will route the application to Planning (already approved via CUA) and assign a plan reviewer; schedule a pre-application meeting with the reviewer. In parallel, submit the building permit application at sf.gov/permitSF with the approved CUA motion, architectural plans stamped by a licensed architect, the DPH plan-check approval, and the fee (percentage of construction valuation, typically $800–$15,000). DBI will route the permit to Planning, Fire, Public Health and PUC for review (2–4 months for full plan review). Licensed subcontractors pull separate electrical, plumbing and mechanical permits.

outcomes.original: Filing step: Before the DPH pre-opening inspection, obtain a Certified Food Protection Manager certificate (ServSafe or equivalent) for at least one owner or employee, and ensure all food-handling employees complete the California Food Handler Card course. What to say: Register for a ServSafe or Prometric food safety manager exam ($100–$250, 1–14 days to schedule and receive results) and pass the exam; DPH asks for the certificate at the pre-opening inspection. All employees who handle food must obtain a California Food Handler Card from an ANSI-accredited provider within 30 days of hire ($7–$15, online course takes about two hours, valid 3 years). Keep the certificate list on site for inspections.

outcomes.original: Filing step: Schedule and pass the DPH pre-opening inspection, then apply for the Health Permit to Operate; in parallel, schedule the Fire Department Place of Assembly inspection (if occupancy is 50+) and the final DBI inspection. What to say: When construction is ~80% complete, contact your DPH plan reviewer to schedule a pre-final inspection at least two weeks in advance; address any deficiencies (missing hand sinks, unsealed surfaces, no hot water are common failures). Once the space passes, apply for the Permit to Operate online with the BAN, LIN, federal tax ID and the food safety manager certificate; pay the $470 application fee (no annual license fee for restaurants in FY 2026–28). DPH issues the permit after the final inspection. If occupancy is 50+, schedule a Fire Department Place of Assembly inspection and obtain the occupancy placard ($446 permit fee). Schedule the final DBI inspection; the building permit is finalized when all departments sign off.

outcomes.original: Filing step: Before opening, register all alcohol servers and managers for California RBS (Responsible Beverage Service) training, subscribe to ASCAP and BMI music licenses, and set up workers' compensation insurance and EDD employer registration. What to say: All alcohol servers and managers must complete RBS certification within 60 days of hire: register on the ABC RBS Portal ($3), complete an approved course ($10–$25), pass the exam, and keep the certification list on site. Subscribe to ASCAP and BMI blanket licenses for live and recorded music (formula-based fees, typically $300–$2,500/year each, sign up at ascap.com and bmi.com). Obtain workers' compensation insurance from a licensed carrier or State Fund (premiums are 2–6% of payroll for restaurant class codes, no government fee); the health and entertainment permits ask for proof of coverage. Register as an employer with EDD at edd.ca.gov within 15 days of paying wages (free, online, 1–7 days).

outcomes.original: Estimated time: 120 to 300 days. Estimated government cost: $6,278 to $21,100. Notes: The day range (120–300 days) and cost range ($6,278–$21,100 in government and application fees) cover the time and fees to obtain the four approvals in the entitlement path when they are granted: Conditional Use Authorization (120–300 days, $3,100–$15,000 per the catalog), Place of Entertainment or Limited Live Performance permit (45–120 days, $2,708–$3,800), Health Permit to Operate (14–45 days, $470–$1,000), and Building Permit with change of use (14–120 days, $800–$15,000). The CUA timeline is the critical path and runs in parallel with the Entertainment Commission permit; the ABC Type 42 license transfer (60–150 days, $1,000–$1,600) begins after CUA approval and runs in parallel with building construction, so it is not added to the day range but its fee is included in a separate alcohol-license line item. The ranges assume the CUA is approved and no appeal is filed; a denial, withdrawal or appeal adds months and is not a time to approval. The cost range includes only government fees and permit application fees; it does not include the cost to purchase the Type 42 license from the source bar (market price, typically $5,000–$50,000+ depending on seller and negotiation), architect and engineering fees for plans ($10,000–$30,000+), construction costs ($50,000–$150,000+ for kitchen, bar, finishes and ADA upgrades), license broker fees (10–15% of license purchase price if used), or legal counsel. ABC's undue-concentration test for census tract 208.01 (28 licenses against 12 authorized) may trigger a Public Convenience or Necessity hearing before the Board of Supervisors, adding 2–4 months; confirm the PCN requirement with SF Planning's ABC liaison before filing.
